title: continuous-batcher-design-notes-token-vs-request
content:
Purpose:
This doc collects design notes, simulation outcomes, and open questions for a continuous batching scheduler focused on token-level vs request-level approaches. Goal is to pick a pragmatic design that:
- meets 99th percentile latency SLOs for interactive chat (target: 150ms per API token)
- maximizes GPU utilization across mixed workloads (short chat, long completions, embeddings)
- plays nicely with KV cache reuse and kernel selection heuristics

Background/context (short):
We currently use a per-request microbatcher (coarse windows) that groups full requests for a fixed scheduling tick. This is simple but suffers head-of-line blocking when a long request (many decode steps) enters the batch and causes other short requests to wait for decoding slots or KV cache thrash.
Continuous batching (token-level scheduling) promises better packing by mixing tokens from different requests into the same kernel invocation, amortizing attention compute. But it introduces fairness questions, complexity in KV cache indexing, and harder accounting for request-level deadlines.

Design candidates (sketch):
1) Request-level windowed batcher (baseline):
   - Collect requests for up to W ms or N requests, then submit per-request decode steps consecutively.
   - Simpler KV cache handling (per-request KV segments).
   - Bad under skewed seq-lens.

2) Token-level continuous batcher (aggressive):
   - Maintain a runqueue of in-flight requests; at each timestep select up to M tokens across requests to build a single kernel launch (pad to model block size).
   - Rotate round-robin with priority aging to avoid starvation.
   - Requires per-request KV slices and careful GPU memory management (evict/reuse).

3) Hybrid priority-driven token batching (practical compromise):
   - Short queue window that opportunistically fills with tokens, but allows some per-request batching if tokens are scarce.
   - Use per-request deadlines (derived from client-level SLO) to prioritize urgent requests at token selection time.

Key considerations and mechanisms:
- Fairness metric: define two axes: latency fairness (percentile across requests) and work fairness (tokens processed per customer in time window). Proposed composite score = alpha * 99P_latency_norm + (1-alpha) * variance(tokens_per_customer).
- Admission control: reject or route non-urgent bulk requests to low-priority lanes (dedicated capacity or background queue).
- Priority aging: avoid tiny requests being deferred indefinitely by increasing priority proportional to wait time and remaining tokens.
- KV cache integration:
   * Token-level mixes require fast access to per-request KV caches. Strategies:
     - Keep KV in GPU memory mapped by request id when possible.
     - If eviction necessary, prefer LRU with prediction-based pinning for requests likely to reuse KVs soon (chat threads).
     - For token-level launches, we need to gather KV pointers per slot; the scheduling path must assemble a compact pointer array to feed kernels.
   * Cost of pointer assembly and memory copies should be measured — may dominate gains for very small token batches.
- Kernel selection tie-in: larger token mixes favor kernels optimized for wide batch dims; short single-request steps favor sequential kernels. The scheduler should expose hints to the kernel selector: expected batch diversity, average seq_len_in_batch, kv_present_ratio.

Pseudocode (token-level selector):
  runqueue = deque()  # requests with tokens remaining
  while runqueue not empty:
    slot_candidates = []
    for req in runqueue:
      if req.deadline <= now + slack or req.priority high:
         slot_candidates.append(req)
      elif len(slot_candidates) < M:
         slot_candidates.append(req)
    sort slot_candidates by (priority + age) desc
    launch_tokens = min(M, sum(req.tokens_remaining for req in slot_candidates))
    build_kernel_batch(slot_candidates, launch_tokens)
    update req.tokens_remaining and requeue if >0

Simulation summary (small synthetic sims run with evt_sim.py):
- Workloads: 60% short chat (avg 8 tokens), 30% medium (64 tokens), 10% long (512 tokens).
- Metric: 99P latency for short requests, GPU utilization (time busy over wall time), fairness variance.
- Results: token-level reduced short-request 99P by ~35% vs request-window baseline at same utilization, but increased variance for large customers (single long requests got slightly worse latency).
- Hybrid (deadline-aware) achieved most consistent tradeoff: ~25% 99P reduction while bounding variance.

Open engineering risks and unknowns:
- Complexity of assembling KV pointer arrays each kernel launch — need benchmarks on real models (Llama2-13B, vicuna-13b q4) to see overhead.
- Effect on token-level billing and accounting (we bill by token; mixing tokens across accounts in a launch must ensure accurate per-request cost attribution).
- Scheduler correctness under preemption and failure: if a kernel aborts, must be able to reconstruct which request tokens were committed; transactional decode checkpointing required.
- Memory fragmentation: per-request KV slices can fragment GPU memory, causing maximum concurrent requests to drop. Consider slab allocator for KV blocks.

Operational/telemetry implications:
- Need new tracing spans: scheduler decisions, token selection reasons, KV pin/evict events.
- New logs for per-launch composition (list of request ids and token counts) — sample heavily to avoid log explosion.
- Evals: integrate with Redwood Optimize to run quality and latency regressions when changing scheduling defaults.

Implementation plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (spike): microbench KV pointer assembly and per-launch overhead on target nodes (2 engineer-weeks).
- Phase 1 (internal beta): implement hybrid token-aware scheduler behind feature flag; add metrics and lightweight sampling (6w).
- Phase 2 (gradual rollout): compare serving economics, fall back to request-mode under heavy long-tail load (4w).

Open questions (to resolve in next sync):
- exact priority function and alpha for fairness composite metric (product decision + infra tradeoff)
- safe eviction policy for KV when under heavy mixed-workload pressure
- how to expose tuning knobs to customers (autosuggest vs manual)

Action items / next steps:
- Ayesha: run KV pointer assembly microbench with 13B models, report copy + assembly latencies by 2025-02-20.
- Claire: extend evt_sim to model per-customer variance and test hybrid priority heuristics (due 2025-02-24).
- Evan: prototype scheduler loop and integrate with kernel selector stub (PR draft by 2025-03-01).

Notes to self: keep design pragmatic — customers care about predictable SLAs more than squeezed utilization wins. Token-level batching is powerful but should be optional/auto-tunable per deployment tier.
